author: ROAPE
title: Life after Museveni, or Uganda beyond fear?
content:
Yusuf Serunkuma’s recent article, 

Life after Museveni

, is an honest expression of a particular political mood in Uganda today: exhaustion. It is the mood of a country that has watched opposition leaders imprisoned, activists disappeared, lawyers forced into exile, protests crushed, elections manipulated and every apparent avenue for change closed one after another. Serunkuma is right to describe the fear. He is right that Museveni has systematically destroyed competing centres of power. He is right that Uganda is facing a political transition. Where we part ways is what he makes of these conditions.




He looks at a defeated and frightened people and concludes that we should prepare ourselves for Muhoozi. He calls this realism, prudence and a search for a peaceful transition. But there is another name for this political position: reformism born from despair. It is the argument that because the forces of liberation have been defeated repeatedly, we should negotiate with the successor of the very system that defeated them. It is understandable. It is also precisely the kind of conclusion that every long dictatorship eventually produces in those who have become exhausted by the struggle.

author: ROAPE
title: Statement of the Finishers Revolutionary Movement
content:
At the beginning of this year, young Ugandans (activists, researchers, academics and lawyers) came together under one roof to confront a question that could no longer be postponed: what becomes of Uganda after the sham elections of January 2026?




With the possibility of Muhoozi Kainerugaba succeeding his father, we gathered around a simple conviction: Uganda must not be handed from one generation of the same ruling family to another. Succession is not liberation. Changing the face at the top while preserving the same machinery of patronage, militarism and corruption is not the future Uganda deserves.




Under the name Finishers Revolutionary Movement, we committed ourselves to organizing Ugandans to reject this succession project and to take up the unfinished work of national democratic liberation.




What we stand for




The Finishers is more than a name. It is an idea: that Uganda’s liberation cannot remain an unfinished historical promise, and that our generation has a responsibility to finish the task. That means we will:







End dictatorship.




Dismantle systems of patronage and impunity.




Reclaim democratic power for the people.




Build a country capable of true economic independence.







What have we done

author: ROAPE
title: Africa’s green stewardship
content:
“First we were dispossessed in the name of kings and emperors, later in the name of state development, and now in the name of conservation” –Indigenous delegation, Fifth World Parks Congress (2003)




I remember that familiar anecdote beneath email signatures during my brief time within the United Nations (UN) system. It read, “please consider the environment before printing this email.” Similar reminders far beyond the UN invoke a familiar ethic of environmental responsibility, particularly around the use of paper and the depletion of natural carbon sinks, namely trees.




Such institutional gestures are largely unobjectionable and even function as legitimising paraphernalia for highly corporatised entities, including NGOs. Much like ethical sourcing labels attached to coffee, clothing and other consumer goods, they can furnish institutions and businesses with the symbolic credentials of environmental stewardship, leaving the structures of production and accumulation seemingly untouched and, by implication, legitimate.




This also speaks to a broader ‘bandwagonism’ within international development, and to the insularity of development professionals when it comes to interrogating the political questions embedded within such global framings. author: ROAPE
title: Who gets to make Ethiopia’s peace?
content:
Ethiopia’s newest opposition alliance contains a remarkable contradiction. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the main party in northern Tigray, now shares a coalition with the Amhara Fano National Movement, although their forces fought on opposite sides of the devastating 2020–2022 war.

[1]

 The Oromo Liberation Army and organizations rooted in Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz also appeared in its founding declaration.

[2]




Announced on 20 September 2026 as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, the coalition seeks Abiy’s removal and an inclusive transitional administration. Its advertised seven-member composition was soon disputed: the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement denied membership on 26 September.

[3]




Removing a government requires agreement about an adversary. Constructing the political order that follows requires agreement about something much harder: who may exercise power, how that power will be limited, what happens to rival armies, how disputed territory will be governed, which crimes from the previous war will be investigated, and who has the authority to write the rules of a transition.

author: ROAPE
title: A demand that can be checked
content:
Africa is not poor. Africa is drained. What changed for the generation that filled Nairobi’s streets in 2024 was not courage but the ability to prove it.




I was raised inside a sentence. Before I could find my grandparents’ country on a map, I had been handed a verdict: it was poor. The word arrived with the settled cadence of fact, and it lodged so early that I mistook it for a thing I had discovered rather than a thing I had been given.




What broke the sentence was not a feeling. It was a number. The continent I had been taught to grieve over is not a debtor to the world. It is a creditor. More wealth leaves it each year than arrives. I had accepted that poverty the way one accepts weather. Weather has no author. A transaction has two parties.




A generation is now doing the arithmetic in public, and it has begun to ask who the other party is.




That question travels further than the ledger. It begins as arithmetic: whose wealth leaves, and by what route. It becomes politics the moment enough people can do that arithmetic at once, which is what happened in Nairobi in June 2024. And it arrives, finally, at the governments that have taken up the same grievance and answered it by making the arithmetic impossible to check. Nairobi and Ouagadougou are not two subjects. They are the same demand at two different stages of what happens when it is made.

author: ROAPE
title: South Africa’s water crisis is about more than water
content:
Komani—formerly known as Queenstown—is a town in the Eastern Cape province, in the eastern part of South Africa. It is part of the Chris Hani District and serves as an important commercial and administrative centre for surrounding rural communities and smaller towns. Its current water crisis is therefore not simply a local inconvenience in a little-known South African town. It is a window into a much larger question facing many countries: what happens when ageing public infrastructure, unreliable energy supply, weak public finances, fragmented institutions and unequal historical development intersect?




South Africa is an upper-middle-income country with sophisticated water infrastructure, major dams, treatment works and publicly owned bulk-water institutions. Yet access to reliable water remains deeply unequal. The country’s democratic Constitution recognises access to sufficient water as a right, while the practical responsibility for getting water from national and regional systems to households is spread across several institutions. This distinction is important: a water crisis can occur even where there is water in dams and substantial treatment capacity, because the infrastructure and institutions required to move that water to households can fail.

author: ROAPE
title: What does Zambia’s Hakainde Hichilema tell us about democracy in Africa today?
content:
Perhaps the strongest hangover from colonialism is the relative lack of consent garnered by the ruling parties: the notion of them gaining “hegemony on a 

shoestring

” in a context where rulers’ goals are to keep labour costs as low as possible in order to expand profits of exports. The strategy depended upon indirect rulers defined by “traditions” (flexible and changing) and regions and required brokerage among shifting alliances. Lacking the ideological means of gaining consent via domination of media and civil society institutions, rulers resort to state violence and intimidation.




In 2021 Hichilema inherited a state structure that had, according to 

Amnesty International

, over the previous decade undertaken a “systematic crackdown on the right to freedom of expression”, criminalizing peaceful dissent and forcing the closure of independent media outlets. One consequence is that there are no reliable sources of information on the current political crisis. What fails to make international news is any analysis of the prominent regional and ethnolinguistic divisions that animate street-level politics. There is also no analysis of the striking absence of any clear differences in ideological or policy orientations between parties. author: ROAPE
title: Africa on the map, but still off the table
content:
On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a non-binding resolution that might initially appear to belong to the relatively technical world of cartography. The resolution, “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa,” was introduced by Togo on behalf of the African Group and adopted by 164 countries, with one country voting against and six abstaining.




In presenting the resolution, Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey argued that maps are not merely technical tools: their repeated use in schools, the media and digital platforms shapes how people understand and visualise the world. The African Group argued that the Mercator projection, designed for specific purposes—especially maritime navigation—had become a general-purpose image of the world that visually minimises Africa and other regions near the Equator.




The delegation framed the initiative around scientific and educational accuracy, cognitive justice, historical memory and the equal dignity of peoples. It also stressed what the resolution would not do: condemn the Mercator projection, impose a single map for every use, alter borders or take a position on territorial claims. author: ROAPE
title: The sports commercializers are in town
content:
Two recent stories from Kenya reflect the rapid growth, rising ambitions, and increasing commercialization and professionalization of East Africa’s sports sector.




In the first, Helios Sports and Entertainment Group, a private equity firm focused on the continent, teamed up with Zaria Group, fronted by former NBA executive 

Masai Ujiri

, to build a $294 million sports and entertainment hub in Nairobi. Then, Oscar-winning actress Lupita Nyong’o 

announced

 she was investing in Nairobi City Thunder, which plays in the Basketball Africa League (BAL).




A few days later, reports said Nyong’o’s investment in Nairobi City Thunder may kickstart further investment in the BAL and sports in Kenya. This was followed by 

more bullish coverage

 of 

further investment

. What do we make of all this? What analytical language and tools do we have to observe and account for these significant on-ground events and dynamics?




One thing is clear: sports and commerce in East Africa are forming ever closer ties in countries such as Kenya and Uganda, across sectors, from rugby, boxing, basketball, and football to athletics, golf, badminton, and motocross, and, lately, e-sports. author: ROAPE
title: Mining in contemporary African underdevelopment
content:
One of the defining characteristics of capitalism is its remarkable ability to emerge from every crisis even stronger.[1] History has shown time and again that war and militarisation serve capitalism’s interests. And even in the case of the climate crisis – for which capitalism bears the greatest responsibility – we are presented with an alleged ‘win–win’ solution. While multinational companies at least partly withdraw from coal mining (see Tsuji et al. 2026, in this issue), the massive rise in 

demand for metals and minerals

 that are needed for ‘clean energy’, digitalisation, consumer electronics, aerospace and militarisation has led to a renewed mining boom, notably of so-called critical raw materials (UNCTAD 2026). In a business-as-usual scenario, demand for these materials between 2024 and 2040 is projected to increase by 353% in the case of lithium, 131% for graphite, 69% for nickel and 49% for cobalt (UNCTAD 2026, 3).




Many of the deposits of these raw materials are located in the global South, with the African continent accounting for about 30% of the world’s critical minerals and metals: for example, 85% of global deposits of manganese (in South Africa and Gabon) and 21% of graphite reserves (in Mozambique, Madagascar and Tanzania).
